Female Bonylip barb (Osteochilus vittatus) reach an ultimate total length of 32 centimeters [Li = 32 centimeters], a size that places them among the larger cyprinids inhabiting freshwater systems across Southeast Asia. Newly emerged larvae are notably diminutive, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0005 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0005 grams], a value that reflects the small egg diameter of roughly one millimeter characteristic of this species. This tiny initial mass imposes a period of high vulnerability to starvation during the transition from endogenous yolk reserves to exogenous feeding in the pelagic larval phase. The larvae rely on a brief lecithotrophic window during which they absorb yolk nutrients before the mouth gape opens and active prey capture must commence. Survival during this period depends heavily on local zooplankton density and water temperature, which influence metabolic rate and the rate of yolk absorption.

Under stable thermal conditions maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum reproductive output of Osteochilus vittatus has been estimated to be approximately 822 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 822 eggs per spawning event], and females spawn multiple times per year [F_R_i = multiple times per year], a value derived from monitoring of spawning females over extended periods in controlled aquaria. This high fecundity per event is consistent with an iteroparous reproductive strategy typical of many tropical cyprinids, which spread gamete production across multiple spawning events throughout the year. Each spawning event produces a clutch of adhesive, demersal eggs that are deposited onto submerged vegetation or other structured substrates. The combination of small egg size and high fecundity reflects a trade-off between offspring size and number, a pattern that is widespread among freshwater teleosts. Females in prime condition can sustain this elevated output across several consecutive months of the breeding season.

Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation and gametogenesis, is attained at a total length of 19.2 centimeters [Lp = 19.2 centimeters]. At this body size, females have typically accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to support vitellogenesis and the energetic demands of spawning. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for females is 84 grams [Wwp = 84 grams], representing a substantial increase from the neonatal mass and indicating that individuals must invest heavily in somatic growth before reproductive activation begins. This growth trajectory is typical of species that delay reproduction until a size threshold is crossed, a strategy that enhances fecundity per spawning event because larger females produce proportionally more oocytes. Gonadal recrudescence is triggered by environmental cues such as photoperiod and rising water levels during the monsoon season.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult females reaches 398.6 grams [Wwi = 398.6 grams], a mass that corresponds closely to the predicted asymptotic body size derived from length-weight regressions in regional populations. This maximum body mass is achieved after several years of sustained feeding and reflects the upper boundary of the species' growth curve. Male Bonylip barb generally attain smaller ultimate sizes than females, a pattern of sexual size dimorphism common among cyprinids that may relate to differences in reproductive investment. The extensive span from the tiny hatchling mass of 0.0005 grams [Wwb = 0.0005 grams] to the adult peak illustrates a growth efficiency that allows these fish to exploit a wide range of trophic resources, from detritus and algae to small invertebrates.

Maximum longevity in Osteochilus vittatus has been estimated at approximately 2,373 days [am = approximately 2,373 days] when individuals are maintained at a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a lifespan comparable to that reported for other medium-sized tropical cyprinids such as Danio rerio under similar laboratory conditions. This extended lifespan allows multiple reproductive seasons and contributes to lifetime fecundity by enabling females to spawn repeatedly over several years. Field records from natural populations suggest that senescent individuals exhibit a gradual decline in condition factor and a reduction in spawning frequency before eventual natural mortality. The thermal environment exerts a strong influence on aging rates, with cooler temperatures typically extending the duration of physiological functioning, although growth rates are simultaneously reduced.
